paras: The lynching of Cornelius Lee took place at or near Plaquemine, Iberville Parish, Louisiana, in February 1903, when a crowd of men took Lee, a Black man, from his bed and hanged him. Lee had been shot on January 25 during a street fight in which, according to white papers, a crowd of Black men beat Andre Gourrier, assistant cashier of the Bank of Plaquemine. Wire reports called him a "dying" man, since gangrene had set in from his wound, and Black weeklies entered him in their lists of the year's lynchings.

On Sunday, January 25, 1903, about six o'clock, Gourrier was walking home from the river bank with his wife and child past Joseph Newchurch's store at the lower end of Plaquemine. According to the Weekly Iberian of New Iberia, he was "set upon and badly beaten by a crowd of vicious negroes," and two white passers-by, M. E. Davidson and G. A. Martinez, were also badly beaten when they came to his aid. More white men soon arrived and dispersed the crowd, and a shot fired in the confusion struck Lee.

In the days after the fight, a Black correspondent writing from Louisiana for the Baltimore Afro-American reported that women living near the scene moved out and that Black residents "prepared for battle." The mayor advised them not to hold church services, and one older man answered that if the whites started anything, "we is gwyne ter finish it."

Lee meanwhile lay in bed with the pistol wound, and gangrene set in. A dispatch from Marshall, Texas, printed in the Houston Daily Post, said he was taken from his bed on a Tuesday night "by a crowd of unknown men and hanged," giving the date as February 18. A New Orleans dispatch of February 19 in The Sun of New York said the mob "broke in" and hanged him to a tree, while Le Meschacébé said he was taken from his home and lynched. The Afro-American's correspondent later wrote that because the man "was to get well," a mob took him one night, hanged him and "filmed [filled] him full of lead."

Coroner W. E. Baker held an inquest that, according to the Marshall dispatch, "developed only the fact" that Lee would soon have died from the gangrenous wound. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of the men who hanged him appears in the coverage.

The first report came from the Weekly Iberian on January 31 under the headline "Nearly a Race Riot," which described Lee as "a surly, impudent, trifling and worthless fellow" and praised Gourrier as "highly-esteemed." When the lynching was reported three weeks later, The Sun ran it as "Lynched a Dying Negro" and the Houston Daily Post as "Dying Negro Lynched," both stating as fact that Lee had "attacked" Gourrier and his wife. The Post's account of the January fight repeated the Iberian's wording nearly word for word, and Le Meschacébé reduced the lynching to a state-news item headed "He'll Not Do It Again."

In the Black press, the Afro-American's correspondent placed the start of the January fight on a white man who cursed a Black man and beat him with a shotgun, and in April set the Plaquemine lynching beside a mob killing at Natchitoches, asking "Is this civilization?" In the summer the Wichita Searchlight and the Sedalia Times printed a list of the year's lynchings credited to The Striker, entering Lee under February 19 with the offense "murderous assault" or "assault." The Seattle Republican ran the same list on August 7 under the headline "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign."

White papers said Black men, or Lee himself, attacked Gourrier without stated cause; the Afro-American's correspondent said a white man cursed a Black man and beat him with a shotgun before the Black man fought back. The shooter is unnamed in every version: the Iberian described a shot fired as the crowd was dispersed, The Sun a passerby, and the Black correspondent a ticket agent who was himself stabbed.
The Iberian also said Lee died the morning after he was shot, but the later dispatches and the coroner's finding describe him as alive until the lynching.

reader.title: Lynching of Cornelius Lee
bases: Three white reports and a Black correspondent say a group of men took the wounded Lee from his bed or home and hanged him (A6, A7, A9, A10).

A 'crowd of unknown men' or 'mob' with no lawful authority took Lee from his bed and hanged him (A6, A7, A10); white reports tie it to his alleged attack on Gourrier, and Le Meschacébé headed it 'He'll Not Do It Again' (A7, A9).

A New Orleans wire (A6), a Marshall, Tex., dispatch with inquest details (A7), a Louisiana weekly (A9) and a Black correspondent in Louisiana (A10) all report the lynching; only the early Weekly Iberian (A1) says Lee died the morning after the January shooting.

accounts.label: Regional white weekly (Weekly Iberian)
accounts.gist: A crowd of 'vicious negroes' set upon Gourrier, Davidson and Martinez for no reported cause; during the dispersal a shot struck Lee, who died the next morning.

accounts.label: Wire reports
accounts.gist: Lee, wounded on January 25 after attacking Gourrier and his wife, lay in bed with gangrene until a crowd of unknown men took him from his bed about February 17-18 and hanged him; an inquest found only that he would soon have died.

accounts.label: Black correspondent in Louisiana
accounts.gist: A white man cursed a Black man, told him to get out of the way and beat him with a shotgun; the Black man fought back, a milkman joined in, and the ticket agent shot the Black man and was stabbed; later, as the wounded man seemed to recover, a mob hanged and shot him.

framing.detail: The Weekly Iberian headlined the fight 'Nearly a Race Riot', called the attackers 'vicious negroes' and Lee 'surly, impudent, trifling and worthless'.
The Sun ('Lynched a Dying Negro') and Houston Post ('Dying Negro Lynched') ran short dispatches stating as fact that Lee 'attacked' Gourrier and his wife, without comment on the lynching.
Le Meschacébé ran the lynching as a one-line state item headed 'He'll Not Do It Again'.
The Afro-American's correspondent blamed a white man for starting the fight and in April set the Plaquemine lynching beside a Natchitoches killing, asking 'Is this civilization?'
Black weeklies carried Lee's name in The Striker's list of 1903 lynchings, introduced as a record of 'mob violence' and, in Seattle, under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign'.
